definition: Faceted search augments lexical search with a faceted navigation system, allowing users to narrow results by applying filters based on a faceted classification of the items.
details: It is a parametric search technique. A faceted classification system classifies each information element along multiple explicit dimensions, facets, enabling the classifications to be accessed and ordered in multiple ways rather than in a single, predetermined, taxonomic order. Facets correspond to properties of the information elements. They are often derived by analysis of the text of an item using entity extraction techniques or from pre-existing fields in a database such as author, descriptor, language, and format. Thus, existing web-pages, product descriptions or online collections of articles can be augmented with navigational facets. Faceted search interfaces were first developed in the academic world by Ben Shneiderman, Steven Pollitt, Marti Hearst, and Gary Marchionini in the 1990s and 2000s. The most well-known of these efforts was the Flamenco research project at University of California, Berkeley, which was led by Marti Hearst. Concurrently, there was development of commercial faceted search systems, notably Endeca and Spotfire. explainer.lead: Faceted search helps people turn a long list of search matches into a manageable one by filtering on properties such as author, language, or format. It combines ordinary text search with several independent ways to describe items, so users can explore results without following one fixed category tree.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a library where you can first ask for books about dinosaurs, then choose only books in English, then only ones with pictures. Faceted search works like that on a computer: each choice removes items you do not want. It uses several descriptions of each item instead of forcing everything onto one shelf.
tiers.practitioner: Build facets through entity extraction from item text or from existing database fields such as author, descriptor, language, and format, then expose them as filters alongside lexical search. This can augment existing web pages, product descriptions, and article collections. Commercial faceted search systems included Endeca and Spotfire; the practical challenge is producing useful classifications from the available text and fields.
tiers.paperLevel: Let each item be classified along multiple explicit dimensions, called facets, whose values correspond to item properties; faceted search combines lexical retrieval with navigation that restricts the current result set by selected facet values. Academic interfaces were developed in the 1990s and 2000s by Ben Shneiderman, Steven Pollitt, Marti Hearst, and Gary Marchionini, with the Hearst-led Flamenco project at the University of California, Berkeley the best-known effort; Endeca and Spotfire were developed concurrently as commercial systems.

explainer.example: In an online article collection, a search for “climate” returns matching articles. Choosing language = English and format = PDF narrows the list, after which an author or descriptor filter can narrow it further.

explainer.intuition: Instead of placing every item in one predetermined category, describe it along several useful dimensions. A text query finds an initial set of matches, and each selected facet value narrows that set.
howItWorks: Classify each item along multiple explicit dimensions called facets.
Derive facet values from item text using entity extraction or from existing database fields.
Run a lexical search to find items matching the user's words.
Let the user select filters based on properties such as author, language, or format.
Narrow the results to items that satisfy the selected filters.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives users several independent ways to refine and order access to information rather than forcing them through a single taxonomic order. Existing pages, product descriptions, and collections can gain this navigation without abandoning lexical search.
misconceptions: It is not merely keyword search: its defining addition is navigation and filtering through a faceted classification.
It is not a single fixed category tree: items are classified along multiple dimensions that can be accessed in different ways.
